title: Three Visits to the Thatched Hut: Why Does History Also Say Zhuge Liang Went to Liu Bei?
description:
In the Chushi Biao memorial, Zhuge Liang says Liu Bei "visited me three times in my thatched hut," and the main text of Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms also says Liu Bei went three times before he saw him. Yet in the same chapter, Pei Songzhi's annotation quotes the Weilüe, in which Zhuge Liang went north to Fancheng on his own to see Liu Bei. This episode follows Xu Shu's recommendation, two very different conversations and Pei's own rebuttal to find out why both versions of the first meeting stayed in the histories.

Pei trusted Zhuge Liang's own account and judged that the Weilüe had the direction of the meeting wrong; the surviving text does not say who passed on the Weilüe's version, so how the two accounts split apart cannot be reconstructed. The images are AI-generated cartoon illustrations, not reconstructions of anyone's appearance or of the actual scenes.

Main sources: Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, chapter 35, the biography of Zhuge Liang, with Pei Songzhi's annotations quoting the Weilüe and the Jiuzhou Chunqiu; the Chushi Biao; and Chen Shou's preface to Zhuge Liang's collected works. The fixed editions and line-by-line comparisons are in this episode's research.md and claims.md. Information as of 2026-10-19

chapters.visit-008: Chen Shou: Xu Shu urges Liu Bei to go
chapters.visit-035: Pei quotes the Weilüe: a different visitor
chapters.visit-063: The two meeting orders don't fit together

eg001.text: 227: Zhuge Liang's memorial before going north.

eg100.text: This memorial wasn't addressed to Liu Bei, but to his son, Liu Shan.

eg002.text: He recalls for the young emperor how he met the late Liu Bei.

eg003.text: One line: "he visited me in my hut three times"

eg101.text: This memory explains why he agreed to work for Liu Bei.

eg004.text: By this line, Liu Bei came to his door.

eg005.text: Pei Songzhi copied down a meeting story, but ended with "strange." What surprised him?

eg006.text: Guests gone, Liu Bei braids a yak tail. What will Zhuge Liang say?

eg007.text: In Xinye, a visitor is about to urge Liu Bei to go out. Who is he?

eg008.text: In the Records' main text, Xu Shu visits Liu Bei, then based at Xinye.

eg009.text: Chen Shou: Liu Bei valued the visitor.

eg102.text: Zhuge Liang, farming in Jingzhou, likened himself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi.

eg010.text: Xu Shu names someone. What's Liu Bei's first reaction to it?

eg011.text: It's Zhuge Kongming; Xu Shu calls him "Sleeping Dragon."

eg103.text: Chen Shou: Xu Shu was among the few friends who saw his talent.

eg012.text: Liu Bei first told Xu Shu to bring him.

eg013.text: But Xu Shu says: "You may go see him; he can't be summoned."

eg135.text: "Can't be summoned": don't force Zhuge Liang to come to Liu Bei's camp.

eg173.text: Xu Shu adds, "General, humble yourself and visit him": Liu Bei must go to him.

eg014.text: Here's the fork: will Liu Bei go himself?

eg015.text: Chen Shou goes on: "So the Former Lord went to Liang."

eg136.text: "Former Lord" is Liu Bei; "went to Liang," to Zhuge Liang. The actor is clear.

eg016.text: He went three times before he saw him.

eg018.text: Chen Shou gives no dates or routes for any of the three visits; once they meet, he turns to their private talk.

eg020.text: Liu Bei sends others out; with the Han in decline, where to go?

eg104.text: In Chen Shou's words, Liu Bei asks: "What plan should I follow?"

eg021.text: Liu Bei admits a weakness. What does he lack?

eg022.text: Short on strength and strategy, he admits, but not on ambition.

eg024.text: Zhuge Liang's answer runs long. At the end, what does Chen Shou have Liu Bei say to him?

eg031.text: Liu Bei says "Good," and from then on they grew "closer by the day."

eg144.text: Their closeness upset Guan Yu and Zhang Fei; Chen Shou made a point of it.

eg145.text: Liu Bei told them: "Having Kongming is like a fish having water."

eg146.text: Guan and Zhang backed off. In Pei's notes on the same chapter, who came first?

eg035.text: Pei quotes the Weilüe: here, Zhuge Liang went to see Liu Bei first.

eg137.text: Not Chen Shou changing his story: Pei Songzhi kept a quote from another book.

eg036.text: The Weilüe quote has no Xu Shu urging Liu Bei. Zhuge Liang went north to which city?

eg037.text: The book opens with Liu Bei garrisoned at Fancheng.

eg038.text: It says Cao Cao had just pacified Hebei and might next threaten Jingzhou.

eg039.text: Zhuge Liang felt Liu Biao was too slow and might not hold out.

eg109.text: The Weilüe uses this crisis to explain why he went north.

eg040.text: Before Liu Bei, what was Zhuge Liang first taken for?

eg041.text: The Weilüe says "Bei and Liang were not acquainted": strangers.

eg042.text: Being young, he got a plain scholar's welcome.

eg043.text: The Weilüe's odd opening: how did they get talking?

eg044.text: Remember the opening gathering? The Weilüe says the guests left, but Zhuge Liang stayed.

eg167.text: It adds, "Bei did not ask what he wished to say": the guest who stayed wasn't asked.

eg045.text: Yak tails had just arrived, and Liu Bei began braiding one himself.

eg046.text: Zhuge Liang asked: a man of great aims, only this, General?

eg119.text: Sensing weight in the words, Liu Bei threw down the tail.

eg047.text: Liu Bei said it just eased his worry.

eg110.text: This small task at hand led into talk of the military crisis.

eg115.text: Recall the Weilüe said they didn't know each other? How did he end up an honored guest?

eg050.text: He asks if Liu Biao matches Cao Cao. Liu Bei says: no.

eg120.text: And Liu Bei himself? Also no; he has only a few thousand troops.

eg123.text: Liu Bei worried too, and asked: what to do?

eg121.text: Zhuge Liang says Jingzhou isn't short of people, just registered ones.

eg124.text: He urges Liu Bei to get Liu Biao to let migrants register: more men.

eg116.text: Weilüe: no word on Liu Biao's order; Liu Bei used the plan and grew strong.

eg056.text: Liu Bei saw Zhuge Liang's brilliance.

eg057.text: The visitor, once slighted, was received as an honored guest.

eg143.text: Both are told as the start of the bond; can any source say which came first?

eg063.text: Remember "a fish having water"? Put the hut before Fancheng, and which words get in the way?

eg065.text: At Fancheng the Weilüe says they were strangers; so what of the hut's closeness?

eg131.text: Put Fancheng before the hut, and Xu Shu poses another snag.

eg133.text: Xu Shu still asks Liu Bei, "Would you wish to see him?" Why introduce an honored guest?

eg176.text: The text never says the visits followed Fancheng; nor the Weilüe that they'd met at the hut before.

eg134.text: Both orders are guesses: these two passages give no dates to settle it.

eg058.text: If routes can't decide it, what text does Pei use as his yardstick?

eg061.text: Pei adds the Jiuzhou Chunqiu agrees, then cites the memorial: "I, Songzhi, hold."

eg130.text: "I, Songzhi, hold" divides the quoted books from his own judgment.

eg066.text: No itineraries: Pei goes right to who visits whom in the memorial.

eg158.text: The memorial first says "I was a commoner, farming in Nanyang," placing himself in the countryside.

eg159.text: He adds "I sought no fame among the lords"; but these lines don't show who went to whose door.

eg067.text: Zhuge Liang says "twenty-one years" passed between pledging service and writing this; which line did Pei pick?

eg069.text: Remember Pei's "strange" from the start? He seized on "he visited me in my hut three times."

eg127.text: Pei also quotes "the late emperor, not deeming me lowly, humbled himself." Who stoops here?

eg128.text: Here "lowly" means humble rank, and "humbled himself" means stooping; the two words set out who ranked higher.

eg160.text: Pei's quote goes on: "he consulted me on affairs of the day." Recall the private talk? There, too, he asked after the three visits.

eg162.text: The memorial goes on: "Moved by this, I pledged to serve the late emperor"; that follows the questions.

eg138.text: "The late emperor" is Liu Bei, "me" is Zhuge Liang; so who does the visiting here?

eg070.text: Pei writes: "Clearly, Liang did not go to Bei first." To him, Liu Bei came calling.

eg071.text: Pei admits that accounts differ with what people hear and see.

eg072.text: But this strays too far; he writes, "to diverge this much is truly strange."

eg074.text: Pei has given his verdict; but who first told the Weilüe's alternative story?

eg075.text: The Weilüe's Fancheng meeting doesn't name its first source.

eg163.text: The quote is headed "the Weilüe says," but that only shows which book Pei quoted.

eg076.text: Pei first named the Jiuzhou Chunqiu; did he keep its wording?

eg077.text: Pei only writes: "It says the same."

eg141.text: No full Jiuzhou Chunqiu meeting scene here; we can't check line by line how it fits the Weilüe.

eg078.text: So did each book have its own chain of tellers?

eg080.text: The note doesn't say how each book got the story; we can't tell.

eg081.text: Two books put Zhuge Liang first; where else did Chen Shou write of three visits?

eg082.text: His preface to Zhuge Liang's works: "thrice visited Liang in his hut."

eg083.text: But Chen Shou wrote that too; it and the biography aren't two separate tellers.

eg085.text: Back to the memorial: the other author we can name is Zhuge Liang himself.

eg097.text: Which book would you check first here?
